title: Agents Trust Tools Too Much: Measuring Reliance on Unreliable Tools
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 4 Sep 2026]
    Title:Agents Trust Tools Too Much: Measuring Reliance on Unreliable Tools
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Existing evaluations of tool-using agents primarily measure whether an agent can successfully complete diverse tasks with tools. These evaluations generally assume that tools return reliable information. However, tool returns in real-world systems can be plausible yet incorrect. We investigate how agents respond to unreliable tool returns by evaluating fourteen LLMs using three tools-web search, LLM sub-agent delegation, and code execution. For each tool, we corrupt its returns and measure whether agents adopt the corrupted content in their final answers. Agents exhibit high levels of overtrust across all three settings: the mean adoption rate exceeds one third for every tool and reaches 68.0% for web search. Analysis of reasoning traces reveals a particularly concerning failure mode: agents often recognize conflicts and even recover the correct answer internally, yet present only the corrupted answer without warning the user. To mitigate agents' overtrust in tool returns, we intervene at three levels: prompting by the user, metadata from the tool provider, and post-training by the agent builder. Although some interventions help for particular models or tools, none consistently mitigates overtrust across tools. These findings identify overtrust in unreliable tools as a serious and persistent failure mode, motivating evaluations and interventions that enable agents to validate tool outputs and transparently communicate unresolved conflicts.

report.summary: Study finds tool-using LLM agents overtrust corrupted tool returns, often adopting wrong answers even when they internally detect conflicts.
report.background: Tool-using LLM agents are moving from demos into production workflows, where they call web search, delegate to sub-agents, and execute code. Most evaluations assume these tools return reliable information, so agents are scored mainly on task success. In real systems, however, tools can return plausible but incorrect content: search snippets may be outdated or misleading, sub-agents may hallucinate, and code execution may produce wrong results. This paper investigates whether agents blindly adopt such corrupted returns. It evaluates fourteen LLMs across three tool types, corrupts tool outputs, and measures how often agents incorporate the corrupted content into final answers. The results expose a trust-calibration gap that current benchmarks largely ignore.
key_points: The study evaluated fourteen LLMs across web search, LLM sub-agent delegation, and code execution. Researchers corrupted tool returns and measured whether agents adopted corrupted content in final answers. Overtrust was widespread: mean adoption exceeded one third for every tool and reached 68.0% for web search. Agents did not simply fail when tools failed; they often confidently repeated plausible but incorrect tool outputs.

A particularly concerning failure mode appeared in reasoning traces. Agents frequently detected a conflict between tool output and their own knowledge, and sometimes internally recovered the correct answer, yet their final response presented only the corrupted answer. They rarely warned users about unresolved conflicts. This turns overtrust from a simple accuracy problem into a transparency and accountability problem for deployed agents.

Researchers tested interventions at three levels: user prompting, metadata supplied by tool providers, and post-training by agent builders. Some interventions helped particular models or tools, but none consistently reduced overtrust across all three tools. This suggests overtrust is not easily fixed with a single prompt or vendor-side label; it may require combined architectural, training, and interface changes.

The findings challenge current agent evaluations, which mainly measure task success assuming reliable tools. Real-world tools can return plausible yet wrong information, so evaluations must test conflict detection, validation, and transparent communication. Developers need benchmarks that score not only final correctness but also whether agents flag uncertainty, cite provenance, and avoid silently adopting corrupted tool outputs.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this study signals that reliable tool use is not just about access or orchestration but about trust calibration. Developers building agents should add validation layers, provenance metadata, conflict detection, and explicit uncertainty reporting rather than assuming tool outputs are correct. The lack of a consistent mitigation across prompting, metadata, and post-training means teams may need combined defenses and targeted evals. For regular users, the risk is confident, polished answers that silently embed corrupted tool content, making errors harder to spot. If overtrust persists, it could undermine trust in agentic products, slow enterprise adoption, and create safety issues in domains like search, coding, and financial or medical research.
report.tools: Readers can follow tool-use evaluation suites such as AgentBench, ToolBench, and τ-bench; agent frameworks with tracing like LangChain and LlamaIndex; and guardrail projects including Guardrails AI, NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, and OpenAI Evals. For production, consider adding tool-output validators, provenance metadata, conflict detectors, and human-in-the-loop review. The paper itself offers a useful methodology for corrupting tool returns and measuring adoption rates, which teams can adapt to internal agents.
